title: The Author of 'Silo' Made Another Sci-Fi Show You Probably Missed — and It's Worth Finding
summary:
If you're a fan of the Apple TV+ hit Silo, you know Hugh Howey's knack for building mysterious, claustrophobic sci-fi worlds. But did you know he wrote another series that got the TV treatment? It's called Beacon 23, and it flew under the radar for most viewers.

Beacon 23 is set in deep space, where a network of lighthouses guides ships past dangerous dark-matter anomalies. The pilot episode kicks off with a starship called the Crest crashing, and its sole survivor, Aster (Lena Headey), seeking refuge at the nearest beacon. But instead of finding a friendly operator, she encounters Halan (Stephan James), a half-mad soldier suffering from PTSD. The two are immediately suspicious of each other, and their animosity drives the early episodes.

As the series progresses, Halan and Aster are forced to team up, fending off pirates and other threats. A mysterious mineral — which Aster wears as a necklace — seems to amplify Halan's hallucinations, and eventually, it coalesces into an alien "Artifact" that appears to have a psychic will of its own. The show weaves in flashbacks and introduces a cast of factions, resistance fighters, and saboteurs all vying for the Artifact's power.

Created by Zak Penn, a Hollywood veteran known for scripts like X-Men: The Last Stand and Ready Player One, Beacon 23 ran for two eight-episode seasons on MGM+ before ending in May 2024. It wasn't a critical darling — it earned a 55% on Rotten Tomatoes from just 11 reviews — but it found a niche audience.

Angie Han of The Hollywood Reporter praised its eerie tone, writing that "those with enough curiosity and patience to wait out its rough patches — and those with a taste for cerebral sci-fi — may find themselves falling under its plaintive spell." The A.V. Club's Manuel Betancourt gave it a C+, but he enjoyed the dynamic between Headey and James, noting that "this unlikely pair come to anchor a provocative new entry in 21st century TV sci-fi fare."

So if you've exhausted Silo and want another dose of mystery-box sci-fi, Beacon 23 is worth seeking out. It may not have been a hit, but it's a hidden gem for fans of the genre.
why_it_matters: Beacon 23 shows that not every good sci-fi show becomes a hit, and that streaming platforms can create space for strange, slower stories alongside blockbusters. For teens, it's also a reminder that an author's original idea can be reshaped in very different ways on screen.

background_read: Beacon 23 also comes from Hugh Howey, the American author best known for penning the Wool novels that inspired Apple TV+'s Silo.

The TV version was created by Zak Penn, a Hollywood screenwriter whose credits include X-Men: The Last Stand and Ready Player One, and it stars Lena Headey (famous as Cersei Lannister in Game of Thrones) and Stephan James (a Canadian actor known for Homecoming and If Beale Street Could Talk).
It aired on MGM+, a premium cable and streaming channel that was once called Epix, and it ran for two eight-episode seasons before ending in May 2024.
The show fits a modern sci-fi TV pattern: a small cast, an isolated setting, and a mystery that unfolds through character conflict rather than nonstop action.
Rotten Tomatoes, a review-aggregation website, shows a 55% score from only 11 reviews, which explains why the show stayed under the radar despite having a devoted niche audience.

perspectives.description: For fans of cerebral science fiction, Beacon 23 offers a moody mystery with two strong central performances. Its short seasons make it easy to binge, and its hidden status could make discovering it feel like a find.

The show was not a critical success, and its rough patches may turn off viewers who expect polished sci-fi. It also never gained a big audience, so the story ends after just two seasons without the cultural footprint of something like Silo.

Beacon 23 is part of a larger wave of streaming sci-fi built around atmosphere and slow-burn mysteries rather than spectacle. Its failure to break out, despite known actors and a famous author, shows how much marketing and luck matter in the streaming economy.

Now that the series is over, discovery platforms like word-of-mouth or social media could give it a second life, similar to other cult shows. If enough new viewers find it, it might even inspire other streamers to take risks on quieter sci-fi.
